overview: Mount Edgcumbe is a Tudor stately home and a big country park on the Rame Peninsula, looking straight across the water at Plymouth. The house was built in the mid-1500s for the Edgcumbe family, gutted by bombs in 1941 and later restored, with its rooms now done up in 18th-century style.

The parkland and gardens are the real draw: they’re some of the earliest landscaped grounds in Cornwall and nationally important, and a favourite with walkers. You can stroll right through the park from the Cremyll ferry and on to Kingsand and Cawsand.

expect.title: The country park
expect.text: Woods, lawns and coastal paths with views over Plymouth Sound, dotted with follies and historic features, including a sheltered anchorage the Vikings used in 997.

expect.title: The house and Earl’s Garden
expect.text: The restored house and the Earl’s Garden beside it open in the summer, from April to the end of September.

goodToKnow.label: Getting there
goodToKnow.text: The main entrance is at Cremyll. A foot ferry still runs between Cremyll and Plymouth, as it has in some form since the Middle Ages.

goodToKnow.label: Ownership
goodToKnow.text: The estate is jointly owned by Cornwall and Plymouth councils, and visitors have been welcome since 1988.

goodToKnow.label: Before you go
goodToKnow.text: Check the official website for current house opening times and prices.

week.text: A good choice for a fine day if you’re staying in south-east Cornwall. Walk through the park to Kingsand and Cawsand for lunch by the sea, or take the little ferry across for a look at Plymouth.

pairWith.why: a pretty seaside village at the end of the park
another historic house across the Tamar inlet

tips: Visit the house between April and September if you want to go inside.
Wear walking shoes and allow time to explore the park on foot.
